newsitem.title: USA: Royal Caribbean closes on rival Carnival with cruise deal.
newsitem.headline: Royal Caribbean closes on rival Carnival with cruise deal.

text.p: Royal Caribbean Cruises Ltd. agreed Tuesday to pay $1.3 billion for Celebrity Cruise Lines Inc., putting the No. 2 operator within hailing distance of cruise-ship leader Carnival Corp.

The merger is but the latest among pleasure cruise-ship companies, scrambling to bulk up for cost savings and marketing power in North America's booming cruise market. Carnival last week completed the takeover of Italian cruise company Costa.

"Celebrity has an outstanding product and reputation, but it hasn't been large enough by itself to take full advantage of those things," Royal Caribbean Chief Executive Richard Fain said in an interview. "We give them scale and size."

Celebrity is the fifth-ranked cruise operator, with some 8,200 berths on its four ships and a fifth, the Mercury, due for delivery in October. Celebrity draws many customers from New England, specialises in expensive cruises a week or longer, and sails mainly in the Caribbean and to Alaska.

Last year, the Miami-based joint venture of Overseas Shipholding Group Inc. and Chandris Group broke even on revenues of $412 million. Royal Caribbean, with 11 ships of its own, had sales last year of $1.37 billion and profits of $151 million.
"Profitability in the industry is becoming a function of size and efficiency," said analyst Scott Barry of Raymond James & Associates. "Celebrity has no economies of scale."
But, analysts said, Celebrity does have a respectable brand name, a solid market niche largely complementary for Royal Caribbean, and a fleet of ships no more than a few years old.
New ships, typically larger and decked out with features such as water slides and nine-story atriums, are increasingly important for attracting cruise passengers.
"Hardware and on-board amenties are very important," Barry said. "The core cruise vacation markets are being dominated by the new tonnage."

Fain and other Royal Caribbean executives said the deal would give the combined cruise lines more clout with suppliers and travel agents booking passengers and permit swapping of routes to improve profits.
Fain said Royal Caribbean would operate both lines separately, with Celebrity Chairman John Chandris staying on.

He said no layoffs were planned but that some staff savings would come in the future because fewer people will be hired by the combined company than the two otherwise would have to take on to meet strong bookings in North America.

Bookings and pricing for cruise operators have been very strong, with Royal Caribbean saying recently it had sold 90 percent of its 1997 berths and was now selling more tickets for 1998 than 1997, analysts said.

By year's end, if the deal is completed, Royal Caribbean should have close to 30,000 berths. It is to take delivery this year of its own new ship for Royal Caribbean, the Enchantment. By 2000, it expects to have 38,000 berths, including those aboard two enormous, 130,000-ton ships due in 1999 and later.

But Carnival, best known for its frenetic Carnival Cruise Line, will have about 50,000 berths by then. Credited with creating the modern cruise-ship business, Carnival also owns the upmarket Holland-America line and others.
Fain said Royal Caribbean agreed to pay $230 million, about 7.4 million new shares, and assume $800 million of Celebrity's debt to complete the deal, and that profits would be hurt next year.
Royal Caribbean shares rose $2.25 to $39.125, a new 52-week high. Overseas Shipping also reached a new 52-week high of $20.125 and was up $1.375 for the day.
